title: Summer berry tart
subtitle: French fruit tart with creme patissiere and fresh summer berries
excerpt: A summer berry tart is a baked pate sablee case filled with chilled creme patissiere and topped with fresh berries finished with an apricot glaze. You get a clean, firm slice with distinct layers of crisp pastry, set cream, and fresh fruit. Watch the creme patissiere as it cooks: it must be stirred constantly or it will scorch on the base of the pan.
sourceNotes: The French fruit tart (tarte aux fruits) is a patisserie classic documented across French baking literature. Pate sablee is the richer, more crumbly alternative to pate brisee, standard for sweet tarts. Creme patissiere as a tart filling appears in Escoffier and in Larousse Gastronomique as a core preparation. The method follows the standard professional approach adapted for home baking.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the pastry case and make the creme patissiere the day before. Keep both refrigerated separately. Assemble and glaze on the day of serving, no more than 2 hours before eating.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 180 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 165 degrees Celsius. Middle shelf for blind baking the pastry case.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rich, short French pastry made with butter, icing sugar, ground almonds, and egg. Sablee means sandy in French, which describes the crumbly, fine-grained texture. It is richer and more tender than plain shortcrust, and is the standard base for French patisserie tarts.

A thick, cooked custard made by whisking egg yolks, sugar, and cornflour into hot milk and stirring over heat until the mixture thickens and boils. The starch gelatinises as it cooks, giving a cream that sets firm enough to hold its shape when spread in a pastry case.

Baking an unfilled pastry case so the crust sets before any filling goes in. The case is lined with baking paper and weighted with ceramic beans or dried pulses so the base stays flat and the sides do not slump.

content.text: This tart has three separate stages. First, make and bake the
pate sablee
case. Second, make and chill the
creme patissiere

. Third, assemble and glaze on the day. None of the stages is complicated. Do them in order. The cream must be properly cold before the berries go on, or it will be too soft to hold the fruit when sliced.

items.prepNote: for creme patissiere, stirred in at the end

content.text: Method
Making the pate sablee

Put the flour, icing sugar, ground almonds, and cold cubed butter into a bowl. Rub the butter into the dry ingredients until the mixture looks like fine sand with no visible butter pieces. Work quickly and keep the mixture cold.

Add the egg and vanilla extract. Mix with a knife and then briefly with your hands until the dough just comes together. It will be softer and more crumbly than plain shortcrust. Press into a disc, wrap, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour.
Blind baking the case

Preheat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius conventional. Roll the chilled pastry carefully on a lightly floured surface to a circle about 3 mm thick. Pate sablee is more fragile than shortcrust; if it cracks, press it back together. Line a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, pressing gently into the sides.
Blind bake

with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes, then remove the beans and bake for a further 8 to 10 minutes until the base is evenly golden and the sides are set. Cool completely on a rack before filling.
Making the creme patissiere

Warm the milk in a medium saucepan over medium heat until steaming but not boiling. Meanwhile, whisk the egg yolks, caster sugar, cornflour, and vanilla extract together in a bowl until thick and pale.

Pour the hot milk onto the yolk mixture in a thin stream, whisking constantly. Return the whole mixture to the saucepan over medium heat and whisk continuously as it comes to a boil. Keep whisking through the boil for 2 minutes until the cream is very thick and pulls away from the sides of the pan. Do not stop stirring or the base will scorch.

Remove from the heat. Whisk in the 20 g of butter until it melts and combines. Pour the cream through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl. Press a sheet of cling film directly against the surface of the cream to prevent a skin forming. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours until fully cold and set.
Assembling the tart

Beat the cold creme patissiere briefly with a whisk or spatula until smooth and spreadable. Spoon it into the cold pastry case and spread to an even layer with a palette knife or the back of a spoon. Refrigerate the filled case for 15 minutes while you prepare the fruit and glaze.

Wash and dry the berries. Hull any strawberries and halve them if large. Arrange the berries over the cream in concentric circles or however looks best, working from the outside edge in. Use the largest pieces at the edge and fill gaps with blueberries.

To make the glaze, put the apricot jam and 1 tablespoon of water into a small saucepan. Heat gently until the jam melts and the mixture is smooth. Pass through a sieve to remove any fruit lumps. Leave to cool for 2 minutes until slightly thickened but still liquid. Brush the glaze over the berries with a pastry brush. Refrigerate until ready to serve.

attrs.heading: If something went wrong
attrs.intro: Three problems that arise with this tart.

items.cause: The cornflour was not fully dissolved before cooking, or the mixture was not whisked continuously.
items.fix: Pass the finished cream through a fine-mesh sieve while still hot. Lumps that go in cold cannot be smoothed out.
items.avoid: Avoid stopping the whisk at any point once the cream begins to thicken in the pan.

items.symptom: Pastry breaks when lifting from the tin
items.cause: Pate sablee is more fragile than plain shortcrust due to the higher fat and almond content.
items.fix: Chill the filled case briefly before releasing from the tin. Release the sides first, then slide the base out once the case is cold and firm.
items.avoid: Avoid trying to release the tart while it is warm or the cream is still soft.

items.symptom: Glaze sets before the berries are covered
items.cause: Glaze was left too long after sieving and cooled past the point where it brushes easily.
items.fix: Work quickly and return the glaze pan to low heat for 30 seconds if it starts to set.
items.avoid: Avoid making the glaze too far ahead; brush it while it is still warm and fluid.

attrs.title: Why press cling film onto the cream
attrs.body: When custard cools, the surface dries and forms a skin. Pressing cling film directly against the surface prevents air contact and keeps the cream smooth throughout. The skin that forms if you leave it uncovered is edible but creates lumps in the finished cream.
